transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

My sleep has been all over the place for weeks, and I can’t seem to get any real rest no matter how exhausted I feel. I just feel completely drained all the time, but my body won't let me actually settle down.
Besides the exhaustion and sleep issues, have you been feeling persistently down, or have you lost interest in activities you normally enjoy?

Yes, absolutely—it feels like someone turned the color down on my whole life, leaving me feeling hollow and on the verge of tears with this heavy sadness in my chest. I've also completely stopped going on my Saturday bird walks and tending to my garden. Even the thought of putting on my boots feels pointless, so I just let the weeds and club emails pile up.
Along with these feelings of sadness, have you also been experiencing constant, uncontrollable worry about various everyday things like your health, work, or family?

I wouldn't say I have constant, uncontrollable worry about everyday things in general. I do feel incredibly stressed and overwhelmed by my husband's health and the mistakes I've been making, but it feels more like a heavy exhaustion and sadness than constant worrying.
You mentioned making mistakes recently. Have you been finding it harder than usual to concentrate, focus, or make everyday decisions?

Yes, I've been struggling to focus and keep things straight, and I feel completely disorganized. It's led to me making mistakes like forgetting quality-control procedures and making errors with radiographs at the clinic, and I've even missed some of my husband's medication times. It makes me feel terrible because I'm usually so meticulous with everything.
You mentioned feeling terrible about these mistakes. Have you also been experiencing strong feelings of worthlessness or blaming yourself excessively for things?

Yes, I feel completely worthless and blame myself constantly. When I make mistakes with the radiographs at work or forget my husband's medication times, I keep thinking I'm a terrible vet tech and an even worse caregiver. I honestly feel like everyone would be better off with someone else who doesn't screw everything up.
Have you ever experienced a period like this in the past where you felt this same level of sadness and exhaustion, or is this the first time you've felt this way?

No, this isn't the first time. These cycles of crashing into deep sadness and then getting highly revved up have been happening on and off for about a year, ever since my husband's heart problems worsened. This current heavy stretch has been dragging on for close to a year now, with only brief breaks where I felt wired.
During those times when you felt "wired" or "highly revved up," did you find that you needed much less sleep than usual but still had a lot of energy, or that your thoughts were racing?

Yes, during those high periods I would only sleep about three or four hours a night but wake up full of energy, feeling like I didn't need any more rest. My mind was absolutely racing with ideas, and I'd find myself talking a mile a minute about new clinic protocols and home projects because everything suddenly felt so urgent and brilliant.
When you had those periods of feeling wired and full of energy, how long did they usually last—would they last for just a few days, a week, or even longer?

Those wired, high-energy periods typically lasted for about a week. During that time, I would feel completely full of energy and only sleep a few hours a night, before eventually crashing back down into a low period.
During those weeks when you felt so wired and full of energy, did this behavior cause any major disruptions at work or in your relationships, or did anyone suggest you needed medical help?

Yes, these swings have caused significant disruptions; at the clinic, my imaging errors actually led to formal write-ups. I've also strained relationships with my friends and running group because I keep canceling on them. It was actually my husband's cardiologist who noticed the toll it was taking and suggested that my mood swings and exhaustion were compromising my health and caregiving, which prompted this referral.

During those times when you felt highly revved up and full of energy, did you do anything impulsive or risky that you wouldn't normally do, like spending too much money, taking unusual risks, or making hasty decisions?

I'm quite embarrassed to admit it, but during those phases I went online and ordered a lot of expensive garden equipment and specialty bird feeders without checking our budget at all. I was also driving much faster and more aggressively than usual between my husband's appointments, justifying it to myself as just "making up time" even though I knew it was really risky.
During those times when you felt highly revved up, did you ever experience things that weren't there, like hearing voices, or did you ever need to be hospitalized?
No, I have never experienced hearing voices or seeing things that weren't there. I have also never needed to be hospitalized during any of those high periods.
When you feel like everyone would be better off without you, have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or ending your life?

Yes, on the worst days, especially when driving back from my husband's cardiology appointments, I catch myself thinking it would be easier for everyone if I just didn't wake up tomorrow. I've even mentally gone through how I could make it look like an accident. It really scares me that my mind goes there.

She describes a history of manic/hypomanic episodes lasting about a week, characterized by a decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, pressured speech, and risky behaviors (reckless driving, overspending) that caused significant impairment (write-ups at work). She is currently experiencing a severe depressive episode characterized by profound sadness, anhedonia, worthlessness, and active suicidal ideation with a plan, without psychotic features. This clinical picture confirms a diagnosis of Bipolar Affective Disorder, currently in a severe depressive episode without psychotic symptoms.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits clear patterns of Bipolar Affective Disorder (F31). She is currently experiencing a severe depressive episode characterized by depressed mood, anhedonia, fatigue, insomnia, concentration difficulties, feelings of worthlessness, and suicidal ideation with active plans. Her history also reveals distinct manic/hypomanic episodes lasting approximately a week, marked by a decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, pressured speech, increased goal-directed activity, and impulsive/risky behaviors (excessive spending and reckless driving). These mood swings have caused significant functional impairment, including formal write-ups at work and strained interpersonal relationships.
